newsitem.title: GERMANY: Speculation mounts Mercedes head may quit.
newsitem.headline: Speculation mounts Mercedes head may quit.

text.p: Speculation intensified Tuesday that the head of Mercedes-Benz AG, Helmut Werner, may resign in what would be a serious loss for the luxury car company, which he turned into one of the most profitable carmakers in the world.

Although Mercedes denied reports that any decision had been made, German media were rife with reports that Werner would step down as Mercedes chairman by the end of the year, the loser in a fight over the reorganization of parent company, Daimler-Benz AG.
Industry analysts said his loss would be a blow to Mercedes, which he has guided back to profitability with a massive overhaul in model strategy.
"It would be negative for Mercedes if Werner was to go," said Sabine Bluemel, analyst at IMI Sigeco. "He has turned Mercedes around."
Speculation that Werner may quit reached a new level Tuesday when the Handelsblatt newspaper reported that he had already prepared a letter of resignation -- a report Werner denied.
Rumours have been circulating for several weeks that Werner may be drafted by Volkswagen AG to help solve its legal battle with General Motors Corp. over allegations of industrial espionage.
Although analysts give the Volkswagen report little credence, there was an increasing belief in the investment community that talk of Werner's departure was not far off the mark.

The debate about Werner's future at Mercedes stem from the plans of Daimler-Benz Chairman Juergen Schrempp to reorganize Daimler, bringing the Mercedes unit more tightly into the group structure and making it less independent.

Werner, whose unit is responsible for the bulk of sales at Daimler, has been reported to be bitterly opposed to the plans, dismissing offers from Schrempp of important jobs in the new group struture and threatening to resign.
Analysts said the loss of Werner, the architect of the most sweeping shift in Mercedes' corporate strategy, would be a blow to the company just as it reaches strong profit growth.

"The financial markets have so far welcomed Daimler's restructuring. But if out of this came Werner's departure, there would be negative threat," said John Lawson, analyst at Salmon Brothers in London.

Werner took over at Mercedes in 1993 when it was deep in the red. By cutting costs and pushing through a broad swathe of new models, he has transformed Mercedes into one of the most profitable carmakers in the world.
